title: Session credit decay hypotheses
content:
Purpose:
Quick personal scratchpad for a session-centric credit model that aims to better align billing with actual serving cost and latency SLOs. Want something middle-ground between pure token billing and monthly seat-style plans that penalize spiky interactive workloads. Not shipping — just back-of-envelope experiments.

High-level idea:
- Sell small bundles of "session credits" where each session starts with a base credit cost (warmup + fixed overhead) and then consumes credits proportional to tokens with a decay curve so later tokens in long sessions are cheaper (KV caching, amortized attention cost).
- Purpose: reflect diminishing marginal cost per token in long-lived conversations due to caching and batching, while still charging for connection/latency-sensitive overhead.

Assumptions (rough):
- Model mix: 70% small-chat (e.g., 7B q8), 25% mid (13B q8), 5% large (70B q4f).
- Average token cost to Redwood (infra + amortized GPU + networking): approx $0.0000018 per token for small, $0.0000036 per token for mid, $0.000009 per token for large. (Very rough, needs validation with infra team / cost table).
- Mean session length: messages per session = 6 (round trips), tokens per message = 40 user + 80 model = 120 tokens per message -> ~720 tokens/session median. Long tail: 95pct < 6000 tokens.
- Connection/warmup overhead per session (startup kernels, KV init, routing) ~= $0.0009 (i.e., ~0.9c) amortized if we count dedicated route + small model startup cost.

Design variants to test:
1) Flat-credit + token multiplier
- Base cost: 1 credit per session (covers warmup).
- Token burn: 0.0002 credits/token for first 1k tokens, 0.0001 credits/token after 1k tokens.
- Pricing: sell 1,000 credits for $10 -> implied price per credit = $0.01.
- Back-of-envelope (small model): cost to Redwood for 1 token = $0.0000018 -> in credits (first 1k): 0.0002 credits * $0.01 = $0.000002 per token billed -> markup vs cost ~1.1x for small model (too low) but ok if most are cached/batched.
- Notes: simple, easy to explain, but token breakpoints arbitrary.

2) Tiered-session product (Conservative heavy-tail protection)
- Each session = base 2 credits + token buckets: first 1k tokens at 0.00025 credits/token, next 4k at 0.00012 credits/token, beyond 5k tokens at 0.00005 credits/token (encourages long sessions).
- Reasons: protect against extremely chatty sessions that are costly if hitting large model; long sessions benefit from KV cache + fewer decoding overheads.
- Example calc: 720 tokens session -> base 2 credits + 720*0.00025 = 2 + 0.18 = 2.18 credits = $0.0218 if credit=$0.01. Hmm that's very cheap — rework required.
- Adjust pricing: if we target $0.12/session ARPU for typical small customer, credit price should be $0.055 -> 2.18 * $0.055 = $0.12 approx. That's one knob.

3) Concurrency-smoothing + burst credits
- Track concurrent sessions per org in 1-minute windows. If concurrency > threshold, sessions during burst burn at 1.5x credit rate. Purpose: reflect capacity pressure & encourage smoothing or upgrade to dedicated.
- Implement as simple multiplier (1x baseline, 1.5x when >90th percentile concurrency).
- Risk: complexity in billing explanation; need UI to show concurrency heat.

Micro-econ checks (sample numbers):
- Suppose a user runs 10 sessions/day, median tokens/session=720, model mix small-only. Monthly active days=22 -> 220 sessions. Using variant 2, credit price $0.055: cost to user/month = sessions*(2.18 credits * $0.055) = 220 * $0.1199 = $26.38/mo.
- Redwood cost: 220 sessions * (720 tokens * $0.0000018) + 220 * $0.0009 overhead = 220 * 0.001296 + 0.198 = 0.2851 + 0.198 = $0.4831/month -> huge margin if these numbers hold. Means either our cost assumptions are wildly optimistic or pricing can be more aggressive.

Sensitivity & knobs:
- Move base credits up if we want to capture more fixed infra costs. e.g., base 5 credits would increase monthly user cost ~2.75x in example.
- Increase credit price rather than per-token multipliers to simplify math for customers (bundle approach).
- Add model-tier multipliers: sessions that use large model mark up credits by 5x. Need detection/labeling at route time.

Unresolved questions / TODO:
- Validate infra cost per token with infra finance slice (get 3-month running average by model family).
- How do we detect "session" reliably for API customers with session-less requests? Could provide SDK helper to declare session id; otherwise fallback to sliding window heuristics (expire after 20 minutes idle). Risk: gaming.
- UI/UX: customers need a realtime preview of how credits are consumed per session. Wire this into Console per-route overview.
- Reconciliation: provide CSV export of per-session burn for accounting.
- Promo/credits for free tier: give 50 session-credits instead of raw tokens to make entry more understandable.

Notes to self (voice):
- This model tries to capture the fact that the marginal cost of later tokens in a session is lower (cache, fewer forward passes on long prefix?) — but double-check with serving runtime team. Might be only trivial improvement.
- Keep experiment small: run credit pilot for a subset of small-model customers (beta flag) and measure realized cost ratio (revenue / infra cost). Aim target revenue:cost = 6x for self-serve.

Quick experiments to run (data asks):
- From logs: sample 10k sessions, compute token-per-session distribution, per-session model mix, and effective per-token GPU time.
- Simulate billing under variants 1/2/3 and compute revenue per org + 90th pct sessions that would hit >5k tokens.
- Correlate concurrency spikes by org to latency incidents (does concurrency > X correlate to tail latency?).

Slack notes/links:
- post early sketch to #pricing for feedback, link to this doc.
- ping @infra-costs for monthly cost table (model_by_size.csv).

Random scribbles (counting):
- If credit = $0.02, base 2 credits => $0.04 per session fixed. With 220 sessions -> $8.8/mo fixed baseline. Good levers.
- If want self-serve ARPU $20/mo for typical developer: set credit price such that 220 sessions -> $20 => overall required per-session = $0.0909 -> if base=2 credits then per-session extra credit budget ~0.0909/0.02 - 2 = -1.545 (contradiction) -> need to raise credit price or base credits. Meaning these knobs interact nonlinearly.

Concluding thought (for now):
- Session-credit model has promise: better productized offering (gives customers a simpler abstraction than tokens) and aligns incentives when sessions have heavy caching. Biggest downsides are complexity and the need for robust sessionization.
- Next step: request log extract and cost table, then run simulation and come back with three candidate SKUs and a small pilot cohort.

End of scratchpad.
